newsitem.title: NAURU: FEATURE - Nauru's wealth hits its health.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Nauru's wealth hits its health.

text.p: The people of the central Pacific nation of Nauru once lived on an island paradise. Today their island looks like a moonscape and their health has deteriorated dramatically.
Nauru people were once amongst the richest in the world, thanks to royalties from phosphate mining on their single island nation.
The 8,000-odd Nauruans still boast a very high per capita income -- US$4,455 in 1996 -- compared with other Pacific islanders, courtesy of US$400 million in trust funds.
But while other nations have increased the life expectancy of their people along with increases in gross national income, in Nauru things have gone into reverse.

Four in five of the islanders die prematurely because of lifestyle-related illness and injuries. Those that survive, struggle with diabetes and weight problems, said Dr Gauden Galea, a researcher from the University of Malta currently in Nauru.
"Most of the premature deaths could be prevented. The main causes are rooted in the lifestyle," Galea told Reuters.
Phosphate mining once made the island wealthy, but the wealth also changed the way Nauruans ate and exercised.
MOTORISTS QUEUE FOR DIABETES TREATMENT

On the busiest strip on Nauru's ring-road, which covers the island's 19 km (12 miles) circumference, overweight motorcyclists and drivers park beside the general hospital to queue up for diabetes treatment.

A few blocks away, families escort a colourfully decorated coffin to a graveyard. Near the single-strip airport, officials collect a van that has crashed against the airport fence during the weekend's popular joy-ride around the tiny island.
"The health situation in Nauru is well below the standard that we wanted," Nauru's Secretary of Health Mark Kun told Reuters in a recent interview.
World Health Organisation research revealed that an average of 78 percent of Nauruans die before they are 65. Men are expected to live to 55 and women to 62.
Nauru also has the world's highest diabetes rate. Local health officials said that more than 30 percent of Nauruans over age 35 have diabetes.
"Since we changed our lifestyle through the influence of Western civilisation, our once healthy and well-built physiques have now developed to be unhealthy and obese," Kun said.
"We took the bad habits of smoking cigarettes, drinking alcohol in excess and eating junk foods."
NO SOIL LEFT FOR VEGETABLES
For almost 50 years, Britain, Australia and New Zealand administered Nauru and jointly mined the rich phosphate deposits -- the result of thousands of years of bird droppings.
Nauru now looks like a moonscape, scared from years of mining, and has very little soil left for growing vegetables. In fact, people are forced to live only on a narrow coastal strip.
For decades the island has relied on food shipped from Australia, New Zealand and Fiji, while increased income has allowed the locals to buy vehicles and stop walking.

Shops offer a variety of tinned food and sweet beverages, alcoholic drinks and cigarettes. Vegetables and fruit are rare and costly. In a fast-food shop in the island's commercial centre, the only vegetable available was French fries.

On average Nauruans are 20 to 30 kgs (44 to 66 pounds) overweight, with a few tipping the scales even heavier, said Filipino dietician Virginia Al-Meaither who works with diabetes patients at the Nauru General Hospital.
She said it was difficult for Nauruans to stop consuming large quantities of rice, cakes, fat meat and sweet drinks as long as vegetables and fruit remained limited and costly.
"There are no food policies regarding food imports, price control or equal distribution around the island," she said.
Foreign health and aid consultants on the island suggest the government should encourage more vegetable and fruit imports and impose taxes on alcohol and cigarettes.

Aid officials said Nauru was discussing imposing taxes on several goods, including alcohol, cigarettes and motor vehicles. These new taxes would contribute US$4.4 million to US$13 million to the budget annually, they said.
HEALTH WOES COST MILLIONS IN OFFSHORE TREATMENT
Each year the Nauru government spends US$3-4 million on treatment of islanders sent to Australian hospitals for treatment.
"We need to promote health awareness to our people and tell them of the consequences of bad habits," Kun said. "The government should support in every way possible all health promotion programmes."
The government recently held a meeting of health and aid workers to develop a "Healthy Island Plan" to improve the health of Nauruans and to reduce a burgeoning health bill.
By 2020 the tiny island's population is forecast to reach 22,000, thanks to a birth rate of seven to eight children per woman.
But if Nauruans simply changed their unhealthy lifestyles they could improve their health, and life expectancy, in possibly five to 10 years, health officials said.
